prime.problem: Design interviews and real designs both fail the same two ways: building the wrong thing because nobody wrote down what "how well" means in numbers, and building something that can't fit because nobody multiplied a few numbers first. The 16 cards each fix one piece; without the map they read as unrelated tips.
prime.fits: This is the course map. It sits before the three parts (framing, object-oriented design, estimation and performance) and ties them with one relationship: the requirements fix the load λ and the target; the design picks the time per request W and how many parts sit on the path.
prime.goal: Draw the whole course as one causal map, from the requirement lists to classes on one side and to arithmetic that rules designs in or out on the other, and say which card settles which decision.

attend: In L = λ × W, which letter do the requirements fix and which one does your design choose?
Why do availabilities multiply along a request path, and what makes a chain of 20 parts at 99.99% miss a 99.9% target?
The functional list becomes classes and the non-functional list becomes arithmetic. Which cards sit on each branch?
In the "what the wrong choice costs" chart, which rows shrink W, which shrink bytes and which shrink D?
Where does the overview say the advice stops applying (averages vs the tail, correlated copies, the crossover below 471,146 items)?

must: Two lists before any boxes → the functional list names nouns and verbs → they become classes and methods; the non-functional list names numbers → they become λ and a target → arithmetic decides which design survives
Load λ (from requirements) × time per request W (from the design) → L requests in flight (Little's law) → pools, threads and memory are sized by L → shrinking W is the design's main lever

Every part a request needs → availabilities multiply → more parts on the path means less availability (20 × 99.99% → 86.3 min a month) → parts need more nines than the whole, and copies help only if they fail independently
An estimate within 10× says the design can't fit → faster hardware, compilers and loop tuning only change the constant → only a better algorithm (a new f(n)) or a new design rescues it
elevated: Python adds a per-object overhead (84 B for a __slots__ node vs 8 B of payload) → the "silent multiplier" that flips 2M records from fitting in 128 MB to 168 MB → estimates in Python must include it
reference: the chart's log-scale bar rule (each 10× = a fifth of the bar)
the book and PEP pointers in "Where to look it up"
the TinyURL illustrative inputs (100M links a month, 100:1, 500 B, 5 years)

compress.prompt: Close the page and draw the course's causal map: start from "two lists", branch to classes on one side and arithmetic on the other, and end at "does it fit?". Put each of the 16 cards where it belongs on the map, and label one number on each branch.
checklist: requirements split into functional (what) and non-functional (how well, in numbers)
functional → OOD branch: classes, is-a/has-a/can-do, rules with their data, policy passed in
non-functional → λ and a target → Little's law and SLO arithmetic
the design sets W and the parts on the path; availabilities multiply
if it can't fit within 10×: change the algorithm (f(n)), not the constant
framing habits (trade-offs, simplicity, robustness, API contract) apply at every step

retrieve.q: Explain why the course insists on putting numbers on the non-functional list before drawing any boxes, using TinyURL's features-only design as the counterexample.
answer: four TinyURL features fit on one laptop with a dict
only "3,858 reads/s, 3 TB, never lose a row" shows that design fails
the numbers become λ and the target that the rest of the course's arithmetic uses

retrieve.q: Walk through the overview's TinyURL chain from 100M new links a month to "requests in flight" and "downtime allowed", naming each step's formula.
answer: L = λ × W = 3,858 × 0.05 s ≈ 193 in flight
derated capacity 3,858 × 6 = 23,148 reads/s

retrieve.q: Your design misses its target by 17×. Rank these fixes by how much they can possibly buy: faster hardware, a better compiler, vectorizing the hot loop, a better algorithm. What does each change in T = c·f(n)/s?
answer: hardware changes s and compilers change c: a fixed factor at every n
vectorizing cuts c by hundreds in Python (58.2 → 0.286 ns per item) but not f(n)
a better algorithm changes f(n), so its gain grows with n
only the algorithm is guaranteed to keep up as n grows; below the crossover the constant can still win

retrieve.q: The overview's chart shows three copies going from 432 min to 2.6 s of downtime, then back up to 21.6 min. What single assumption breaks, and which formula stops applying?
answer: 1 − (1 − p)^k assumes copies fail independently
a shared 99.95% layer (config push, power) sits in series with all three
the shared layer sets the floor: 0.9995 × 0.999999 ≈ 0.9995

compare.q: The series map places cs-4 as the course with no prerequisites that cs-5 and cs-6 need. Which two tools from this course does cs-5 lean on most, and what would a reader who skipped cs-4 misjudge there?
answer: requirements as numbers and the SLO/downtime arithmetic
estimation habits: Little's law and derating
without them, replication looks free: pᴺ seems to buy any reliability, and sizing becomes guessing

compare.q: This course's formula multiplies availabilities as if parts fail independently; cs-5's map is built around what happens when they don't. What is fundamentally different in how each course treats a failure, and when is this course's arithmetic still the right first step?
answer: here: failures are independent and averaged, so arithmetic on nines is enough
cs-5: partial and correlated failures, where copies share a fate and the network is silent
still right first: to budget the error minutes and to see that serial parts need extra nines, before asking what the copies share

predict.q: TinyURL's read rate doubles to 7,716/s and the median request time stays 50 ms, but the p99 time is 10× the mean. Before checking: does Little's law tell you how many connections you need at the worst moment? Commit to yes or no, and to what it does tell you.
predict.answer: No. Little's law gives the average number in flight: 7,716 × 0.05 ≈ 386 (twice 193). It says nothing about the tail. Bursts and slow requests push the instantaneous count well above that average, which is why the back-of-envelope card derates (Roebling's 6×) and the averages card says to report the median and tail percentiles, not only the mean.

apply.task: Size a new illustrative service with the course's tools: a paste-sharing site with 10M new pastes a month, 10:1 reads to writes, 10 KB per paste, kept 1 year, 30-day months. (1) Write both requirement lists (3 lines each). (2) Compute writes/s, reads/s and storage. (3) With 50 ms per read, compute L. (4) The read path has 4 parts at 99.99% and a database at 99.95%: compute its monthly downtime and say whether it meets 99.9%. (5) Name one class from the functional list that owns a rule, and one policy you'd pass in.
apply.done: Your numbers are 3.86 writes/s, 38.6 reads/s, 1.2 TB, L ≈ 1.9 in flight, and availability 0.9999⁴ × 0.9995 ≈ 0.99910, which is 38.9 min a month and meets 99.9% with about 4 minutes to spare.
